Ghana’s Electric Utilities Industry Faces Widespread Disruption as Workers Strike

Accra, June 26 — Ghana’s electric utilities industry is experiencing significant operational disruptions as unionized workers began an indefinite strike Wednesday morning, pressing demands for improved wages and better safety conditions. The walkout, which commenced at 6:00 a.m. local time, has affected major power providers, including Electricity Co Of Ghana Ltd and several regional distribution firms.

The Ghana Energy Workers Union (GEWU), which represents over 9,000 workers across the country’s electric utilities sector, announced the strike late Tuesday after negotiations with the Ministry of Energy stalled. “Our members are united in seeking a fair resolution to long-standing compensation and safety concerns,” GEWU General Secretary Samuel Tetteh Nartey said in a statement. “Until there is meaningful engagement from management, the strike will continue.”

As of Wednesday afternoon, the strike had forced numerous substations to operate on limited staff, leading to reports of delayed response times to outages and routine maintenance. Electricity Co Of Ghana Ltd confirmed in a press release that its service centers in Accra, Kumasi, and Takoradi are operating with skeleton crews and that restoration of power in affected areas may be delayed. “We are prioritizing emergency repairs and critical infrastructure, but customers should expect longer waiting times for non-essential services,” the company stated.

Industry analysts estimate that up to 65% of the nation’s distribution capacity could be affected if the strike persists. “The electric utilities industry in Ghana is highly labor-dependent, and prolonged industrial action poses a risk of escalating grid instability and deferred maintenance,” said Kwabena Mensah, a utilities analyst at Accra-based consultancy VoltEdge Analytics. 

The Ghana Electric Utilities Association has urged both sides to return to negotiations, warning that continued disruption could undermine public confidence in the reliability of the country’s power infrastructure. “We recognize the legitimacy of workers’ concerns, but a swift resolution is critical to ensure service continuity,” said association president Gloria Owusu.

Government officials have called for calm and pledged to facilitate renewed talks between the union and industry representatives. However, as of the time of writing, there had been no formal announcement of new negotiations.

With the strike ongoing and no immediate breakthrough in sight, electric utilities across Ghana are bracing for further operational challenges in the coming days.
